etymologies.etymologyHTML: First attested from 1300, from Middle English merveile, from Old French merveille (“a wonder”), from Vulgar Latin *miribilia, from Latin mīrābilia (“wonderful things”), from neuter plural of mīrābilis (“strange, wonderful”), from mīror (“I wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”). Doublet of mirabilia.

definitions.definition: That which causes wonder; a prodigy; a portent.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XXIV, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume II, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 261:
quote.text: The mysteries of this wonderful universe rise more palpable upon the departing spirit, so soon to mingle with their marvels.

quote.citation: 2017 December 1, Tom Breihan, “Mad Max: Fury Road might already be the best action movie ever made”, in The Onion AV Club‎[1]:
quote.text: He found ways to film fiery, elaborate car-wrecks, keeping everything visually clear and beautiful without killing or even seriously injuring anyone. On a sheer technical level, the movie is a marvel.

quote.citation: 1805, Walter Scott, “(please specify the page)”, in The Lay of the Last Minstrel: A Poem, London:  […]  [James Ballantyne] for Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], and A[rchibald] Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive, used impersonally) To cause to wonder or be surprised.
(intransitive) To become filled with wonderment or admiration; to be amazed at something.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 John 3:13, column 1:
